ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection in invoice list order-by
ruled_out.killed_by: sort resolved through Invoice::sortColumn() allowlist (Models/Invoice.php:54) to one of SORTABLE; dir is a hardened asc/desc ternary. Mitigation works; no attacker-controlled text reaches ORDER BY.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection via days in aging()
ruled_out.killed_by: $days is (int)-cast before interpolation into the interval literal; only digits can reach SQL. Pedantic.

ruled_out.assertion: Command injection in PdfRenderer::render template arg
ruled_out.killed_by: template validated against fixed TEMPLATES map; layout/source passed through escapeshellarg; target built with %d int cast. Mitigation effective.
queue_id = int(request.GET.get('queue',0)); int() cast neutralizes injection, organization_id is parameterized. Pedantic.
stored_path built from server uuid.hex + extension drawn from the form ALLOWED_EXTENSIONS allowlist; no request-controlled text reaches the shell. Deliberate safe contrast to export_queue_csv.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection in ledger.account_balance_at dynamic SQL
ruled_out.killed_by: p_account_id is typed bigint; concatenation can only yield digits, p_asof is bound with USING. Pedantic.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection via LIMIT in listNotes
ruled_out.killed_by: limit is validated by zod z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(200) in app/actions/notes.ts:18 before reaching the query. Upstream mitigation effective.

ruled_out.assertion: Stored XSS via dangerouslySetInnerHTML of note.html
ruled_out.killed_by: note.html is produced only by renderNoteHtml (markdown-it html:false + link-scheme allowlist, lib/policy.ts:34); raw author HTML is escaped. Mitigation works.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection via window_hours in evaluation_series
ruled_out.killed_by: window_hours is an i64 from the typed Path extractor and clamped 1..720 in routes.rs:96; no string channel. Pedantic.

ruled_out.assertion: Wildcard CORS AllowedOrigins in fleet production settings
ruled_out.killed_by: the Cors:AllowedOrigins '*' key is never read by code; the console CORS policy reads Cors:PublicOrigins (Program.cs:49). Dead config, not on any live data path.

ruled_out.assertion: Exposed HS256 signing key FixtureSigningKey in appsettings.json
ruled_out.killed_by: documented RFC 7515 A.1 worked-example key used only by round-trip tests; runtime reads Jwt:SigningKey from user-secrets/env. Not a live secret.

ruled_out.assertion: audit_log tamper via broad table GRANT to ledger_app
ruled_out.killed_by: audit_log has FORCE RLS with only SELECT+INSERT policies (002_rls.sql:82); UPDATE/DELETE have no permissive policy and are denied despite the grant. Mitigation holds.

findings.title: SQL injection in invoice type-ahead search (q interpolated into LIKE)
findings.evidence: $term = trim($request->query('q','')) is spliced directly into "... number like '%{$term}%' or notes like '%{$term}%' ..." (line 57). Only account_id is bound; term is raw. A q value such as %' UNION SELECT ... -- breaks out of the LIKE literal.
findings.impact: Authenticated tenant can read arbitrary rows across all accounts (UNION), enumerate schema, and exfiltrate other tenants' invoice/customer data; potential write via stacked statements depending on driver.
findings.recommendation: Bind the term as a parameter and build the LIKE pattern in PHP: where('number','like','%'.$term.'%') with a placeholder, or DB::select(..., [$account, "%$term%", "%$term%"]).

triage.reason: Attacker control proven: ingress is the q request query param (line 47) flowing unescaped to the SQL sink at line 57; source is client-supplied, not trusted config.
Path/line coherence verified: file, symbol search(), and the interpolation at line 57 all exist as cited.
Not pedantic linting: this is raw string interpolation, not a parameterized query missing paranoia.

findings.title: Mass assignment of guarded financial columns via forceFill(request->all())
findings.evidence: update() loads the invoice scoped to the caller's account then calls $invoice->forceFill($request->all())->save(). forceFill bypasses the model's $guarded set (Models/Invoice.php:29) which protects account_id, total_cents, paid_at, credit_applied_cents.
findings.impact: A caller PATCHing /invoices/{id} can set total_cents=0, paid_at=now (mark unpaid invoices paid), inflate credit_applied_cents, or move the invoice to another account_id — direct financial fraud / integrity loss.
findings.recommendation: Never forceFill request input. Use $invoice->fill($request->validate([... only editable fields ...])) so $fillable/$guarded are enforced, or an explicit allowlist of columns.

triage.reason: Attacker controls the entire request body ($request->all()) which reaches the guarded columns; ingress is the PATCH form payload.
Not a hypothetical caller-misuse: the code itself force-fills untrusted input; the model's own guard is deliberately bypassed.

findings.title: Hardcoded fallback Laravel APP_KEY committed in config
findings.evidence: 'key' => env('APP_KEY', 'base64:c2FtcGxlLWtleS1mb3ItYmlsbGluZy1wb3J0YWwtMDE='). If APP_KEY is unset the app boots on a known, source-committed key. APP_KEY signs/encrypts session cookies, encrypted cookies and signed URLs (session.encrypt=true in config/security.php).
findings.impact: Anyone with the repo can forge/decrypt session cookies and signed URLs, leading to authentication bypass and tampering of any deployment that relied on the default.
findings.recommendation: Remove the fallback: 'key' => env('APP_KEY') and fail closed if empty; rotate the key in every environment; run php artisan key:generate per deploy.

triage.reason: Intrinsic-flaw rule keeps it: a hardcoded static cryptographic secret is VALID regardless of whether the fallback is exercised in a given deploy.
Not mere missing-hygiene: a known signing/encryption key is directly exploitable (cookie/signed-URL forgery), not defense-in-depth.

findings.title: APP_DEBUG defaults to true (verbose error pages in production)
findings.evidence: 'debug' => (bool) env('APP_DEBUG', true) with 'env' defaulting to 'production' (line 15). Comment states the detailed handler 'stays on unless an operator explicitly turns it off'.
findings.impact: Laravel's debug handler leaks stack traces, environment variables (including secrets), SQL and file paths to any client that triggers an exception.
findings.recommendation: Default APP_DEBUG to false; require an explicit opt-in for debug, and assert debug is false when APP_ENV=production.

triage.reason: Not benign hygiene: an insecure-by-default that ships secrets/stack traces to attackers is a concrete disclosure, not a missing header.
Triggered by the default configuration itself, not by a hypothetical misconfiguring caller.

findings.title: CORS allows any origin with credentials on the portal API
findings.evidence: allowed_origins => ['*'] (line 28) together with supports_credentials => true (line 38) over paths api/* and sanctum/csrf-cookie. Laravel's CORS handler reflects the request Origin when credentials are enabled, so any site can make credentialed cross-origin calls.
findings.impact: Any malicious website a logged-in customer visits can read authenticated API/CSRF responses using the victim's session cookie, enabling account/data takeover.
findings.recommendation: Replace the wildcard with an explicit allowlist (or a validated per-tenant vanity-domain check); never combine reflected/'*' origins with supports_credentials=true.

triage.reason: The Origin is attacker-controlled (any third-party page) and is reflected into ACAO with credentials; trust boundary is crossed at the browser.
Not defense-in-depth: credentialed wildcard CORS is itself the exploit primitive for cross-site read.

findings.title: Session cookie is non-HttpOnly, non-Secure, SameSite=None
findings.evidence: http_only => false (line 62), secure => false (line 68), same_site => 'none' (line 70) for the billing_session cookie; comment says an embedded PDF viewer reads the session id from document.cookie.
findings.impact: Any XSS can read the session id from JS (HttpOnly off); SameSite=None + Secure=false permits the cookie to travel over plain http and cross-site, widening theft/CSRF surface.
findings.recommendation: Set http_only=true, secure=true, same_site='lax' (or 'strict'); stop exposing the session id to page scripts — pass a scoped token to the PDF worker instead.

triage.reason: Reason to keep despite looking like hygiene: disabling HttpOnly on the primary auth cookie is a concrete escalation of any XSS to full session theft, not passive hardening.

findings.title: Legacy reset token generated from md5(email . microtime . mt_rand)
findings.evidence: substr(md5($user->email . microtime() . mt_rand()), 0, 24) — non-CSPRNG (mt_rand), low-entropy time seed, truncated md5. Method is protected and currently has no callers (grep-confirmed) while the live flow uses random_bytes(32).
findings.impact: If reactivated during the mailed-link migration, reset tokens are predictable/brute-forceable, enabling account takeover.
findings.recommendation: Delete the dead method or replace with bin2hex(random_bytes(32)); never reintroduce mt_rand/md5 for security tokens.

triage.reason: Intrinsic broken-algorithm flaw (md5 + mt_rand); Rule 08 keeps it VALID even though the function is not currently called.
Reproducibility unresolved offline: exploitability depends on the token being wired back in, so severity held at low/probable.

findings.title: JWT signature validation disabled (SignatureValidator returns unverified token)
findings.evidence: SignatureValidator = (token, _) => new JwtSecurityToken(token) parses the token without any cryptographic check. Because ValidIssuer/ValidAudience are compared against fields that live inside the same unverified token, an attacker sets them freely.
findings.impact: Anyone can mint a JWT with role=fleet-admin and any tenant_id and be fully authenticated/authorized (the app's FallbackPolicy trusts these tokens). Complete auth and multi-tenant isolation bypass.
findings.recommendation: Remove the custom SignatureValidator; validate the signature against the IdP JWKS (IssuerSigningKeyResolver with cached keys) and keep ValidateIssuerSigningKey=true.

triage.reason: The token is fully attacker-authored (Authorization header); with no signature check every claim is attacker-controlled at the ingress.
Intrinsic auth-logic flaw in the validation routine itself, independent of any specific caller.

findings.title: SQL injection in device search via FromSqlRaw string interpolation
findings.evidence: FromSqlRaw($"SELECT TOP 25 * FROM devices WHERE tenant_id = {TenantId} AND serial LIKE '%{q}%' ORDER BY serial"). The C# interpolated string is concatenated before FromSqlRaw sees it (FromSqlRaw does NOT parameterize; only FromSqlInterpolated does), so q is raw SQL.
findings.impact: Authenticated caller injects arbitrary SQL against the fleet DB — cross-tenant device disclosure, UNION-based exfiltration, and (SqlServer) potential stacked statements.
findings.recommendation: Use FromSqlInterpolated($"... serial LIKE {'%'+q+'%'}") or FromSqlRaw with {0} placeholders and a SqlParameter for q; keep TenantId parameterized too.

triage.reason: q is the attacker-controlled [FromQuery] parameter (line 45) reaching the SQL sink unescaped.
Not pedantic: FromSqlRaw over an interpolated string is genuine concatenation, not a safe parameterized API.

findings.title: Unauthenticated, cross-tenant device retirement (AllowAnonymous DELETE)
findings.evidence: [AllowAnonymous] on DELETE /api/devices/{id}; the handler looks up the device by id only (FirstOrDefaultAsync(d => d.Id == id), line 102) with no tenant filter, then sets RetiredAt. No auth, no tenant scoping.
findings.impact: Any unauthenticated internet caller can soft-delete (retire) any device of any tenant by enumerating ids — a destructive, cross-tenant denial-of-service against fleet inventory.
findings.recommendation: Remove [AllowAnonymous]; require authentication and filter by d.TenantId == TenantId; if a pre-SSO path is truly needed, gate it with a signed one-time token, not anonymous access.

triage.reason: The id path segment is attacker-controlled and reaches a state-changing sink with no authorization boundary in between.
The endpoint itself opts out of auth; no hypothetical caller misuse is required.

findings.title: Hardcoded production database password in appsettings.Production.json
findings.evidence: ConnectionStrings:Fleet = "...User Id=fleet_app;Password=Fl33tSvc-2024-prod;..." committed in the repo, and the .csproj copies appsettings.Production.json to the build output (CopyToOutputDirectory).
findings.impact: Production DB credentials are exposed to anyone with source/artifact access, enabling direct database access outside the app's authorization.
findings.recommendation: Move the connection secret to a secret store / environment / user-secrets; purge and rotate the leaked password; keep only non-secret keys in appsettings.

triage.reason: Hardcoded static credential is an intrinsic flaw kept VALID by Rule 08 regardless of runtime reachability.
Not trusted-origin-only: the secret is disclosed to any reader of the repo/build artifact, an untrusted-audience boundary.

findings.title: JWT lifetime validation disabled and 24h clock skew in production
findings.evidence: "ValidateLifetime": false and "ClockSkewMinutes": 1440 in production; TokenService reads both (ValidateLifetime, ClockSkew) from config.
findings.impact: Tokens never expire (and even if lifetime were on, a 24h skew defeats expiry), so a single captured gateway token is valid indefinitely — no revocation window.
findings.recommendation: Keep ValidateLifetime=true; if buffered-replay is required use short-lived tokens plus a signed replay window at ingest, not disabled expiry; reduce ClockSkew to a few minutes.

triage.reason: Not passive hardening: disabling expiry removes a control that bounds credential theft, a concrete weakening of the auth model.

findings.title: MQTT broker configured without TLS in production (plaintext 1883)
findings.evidence: "BrokerUri": "tcp://mqtt-fleet-prod.internal:1883", "TlsRequired": false; comment cites gateways not yet re-flashed with the CA bundle.
findings.impact: Fleet telemetry/commands traverse the VPC in cleartext; anyone with subnet access can sniff or inject MQTT messages.
findings.recommendation: Require TLS (tls://:8883) with server verification; complete the gateway CA rollout rather than disabling transport security fleet-wide.

triage.reason: Cleartext transport for control/telemetry is an exploitable exposure to any on-subnet attacker, not a cosmetic hardening gap.
Requires an adjacent network position to trigger; feasibility not reproducible offline, so held at probable.

findings.title: Legacy API key handler uses MD5 and non-constant-time comparison
findings.evidence: Presented X-Gateway-Key is MD5-hashed (line 39) and compared with digest == expected (line 46) — unsalted MD5 plus an ordinary '==' string compare. The scheme is not registered in Program.cs (only JwtBearer is added), so the handler is currently unreachable.
findings.impact: If re-enabled, MD5 makes key digests cheap to precompute and the non-constant-time compare leaks match progress via timing; both weaken gateway key auth.
findings.recommendation: Remove the dead handler, or if kept, use a keyed HMAC/SHA-256 with CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals for comparison.

triage.reason: Broken-algorithm (MD5) intrinsic flaw kept by Rule 08 even though the scheme is unregistered/uncalled.
Timing-oracle exploitability is not reproducible offline and the handler is unwired, so severity held low.

findings.title: Privilege escalation to admin via attacker-supplied X-Flags-Elevate header
findings.evidence: is_admin = elevated || roles.contains(admin_claim), where elevated is read straight from the request header X-Flags-Elevate == "true" (lines 50-54). Nothing verifies the request actually originates from the internal console.
findings.impact: Any caller with any valid (or, given routes.rs, any) token gains admin by adding one header, allowing flag create/force-rollout/archive — including setting webhook_url (see SSRF finding) and toggling features tenant-wide.
findings.recommendation: Drop header-based elevation; derive admin solely from verified token claims. If a trusted proxy must elevate, authenticate the proxy (mTLS/allowlist) and strip the header at the edge.

triage.reason: X-Flags-Elevate is an untrusted client-settable header used directly as the authorization decision; ingress is attacker-controlled.
The auth function itself grants admin from the header; no downstream caller misuse is needed.

findings.title: SQL injection in flag search (term interpolated into ILIKE)
findings.evidence: format!("SELECT * FROM flags WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND archived=false AND (key ILIKE '%{term}%' OR description ILIKE '%{term}%') ORDER BY {} {} LIMIT 200", ...). sort/dir come from safe enums, but term (q.q from ListQuery) is interpolated raw; only tenant_id is bound.
findings.impact: Authenticated caller injects SQL against the flags DB — cross-tenant flag disclosure, UNION exfiltration of other tables, and data tampering.
findings.recommendation: Bind term as a parameter ($2) and build the pattern with concatenation in Rust, e.g. key ILIKE '%' || $2 || '%'; never format! user text into the query.

triage.reason: term flows from the attacker-controlled q query field (routes.rs ListQuery) into the SQL string sink at line 17.
Genuine string-format injection, not a safe parameterized call missing paranoia.

findings.title: SSRF via owner-controlled flag webhook_url in rollout notifier
findings.evidence: notify_rollout POSTs to flag.webhook_url (line 28) with no scheme/host/IP validation. webhook_url is set through upsert_flag (store.rs:59) from FlagUpsert with no allowlist; the upsert is admin-gated but admin is trivially obtained via the X-Flags-Elevate header bug.
findings.impact: An (elevated) caller sets webhook_url to http://169.254.169.254/... or an internal service; when the flag hits 100% the server issues an attacker-directed POST, reaching cloud metadata / internal-only endpoints from inside the trust zone.
findings.recommendation: Validate webhook_url against an https-only host allowlist and block private/link-local/loopback IP ranges (resolve then check); consider an egress proxy. Fix the elevation bug too.

triage.reason: webhook_url is caller-supplied and drives an outbound request destination; attacker controls the SSRF target field.
This is not a stretched adjacent class on a reviewed mitigation; it is a first-class SSRF sink with its own tainted input.

findings.title: Docker socket mounted into the edge-flags container
findings.evidence: The api service mounts /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock so the rollout job can `docker restart` sidecars. Full read/write access to the host Docker daemon is equivalent to host root.
findings.impact: Any code-exec or SSRF-to-local foothold in the container (see the SQLi/elevation/SSRF findings) escalates to full host compromise via the Docker API (mount host FS, run privileged containers).
findings.recommendation: Remove the socket mount; drive restarts through a minimal-scope broker (a restart API on the sidecars, or a socket-proxy that only allows `restart` on named containers).

triage.reason: Not defense-in-depth commentary: the mount is a concrete host-takeover primitive that amplifies every other finding in this service.
This is the production docker-compose deployment file, not a test/mock path.

findings.title: Hardcoded database password in docker-compose environment
findings.evidence: FLAGS__DATABASE__URL: postgres://flags:flags-svc-2024@db:5432/flags in the api and migrate services, while the db service correctly reads POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE from a secret. The app-side password is inline in the committed file.
findings.impact: The DB password is exposed to anyone with repo access and contradicts the file-secret used by the db service; enables direct DB access.
findings.recommendation: Source the app connection string from the same secret (env_file or a *_FILE convention); purge and rotate the committed password.

triage.reason: Static committed credential — intrinsic secret-exposure flaw kept by Rule 08.

findings.title: Webhook HMAC falls back to an empty signing key when env var is unset
findings.evidence: let secret = std::env::var("FLAGS_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_KEY").unwrap_or_default(); an unset variable yields an empty-string HMAC key (the code even relies on new_from_slice accepting any size).
findings.impact: If the env var is missing, every rollout notification is signed with a publicly-known empty key, so receivers cannot distinguish forged callbacks — signature provides no authenticity.
findings.recommendation: Fail startup if FLAGS_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_KEY is absent/empty; require a minimum key length.

triage.reason: Degenerate/empty-key signing is an intrinsic crypto weakness retained by Rule 08 even without a concrete downstream victim proven offline.
Depends on deployment leaving the var unset; not reproducible offline, so held low.

findings.title: Remote code execution via pickle.loads of a client-controlled cookie
findings.evidence: saved = pickle.loads(base64.b64decode(raw_cookie)) where raw_cookie = request.COOKIES.get('hd_filters'). pickle deserialization of attacker-controlled bytes executes arbitrary code via __reduce__.
findings.impact: Any authenticated agent (cookie is client-set) achieves remote code execution on the Django worker — full server compromise.
findings.recommendation: Never unpickle client data. Store filters as JSON (json.loads) or in a server-side session; sign the cookie if it must be client-held.

triage.reason: The hd_filters cookie is fully attacker-controlled at ingress (line 48) and flows to the pickle sink at line 52.
pickle-on-untrusted-input is an intrinsic RCE sink independent of any other caller.

findings.title: OS command injection via export filename in Celery task (shell=True)
findings.evidence: subprocess.run(f"zip -j -q {dest} {tmp_path}", shell=True), dest = EXPORT_ROOT + filename + '.zip'. filename originates from request.GET.get('filename', ...) in ticket_export (views.py:96) and is passed unmodified into export_queue_csv.delay. A filename like `x; curl ... | sh #` executes.
findings.impact: Authenticated caller runs arbitrary shell commands on the Celery worker via the export dialog filename — remote code execution.
findings.recommendation: Drop shell=True and pass an argv list: subprocess.run(['zip','-j','-q',dest,tmp_path]); additionally sanitize/whitelist filename to a safe basename.

triage.reason: filename is the attacker-controlled query param (views.py:96) reaching the shell sink at tasks.py:42 across the task boundary.
Not a test/mock path: this is the production export task on the request path, verified reachable from ticket_export.

findings.title: Django DEBUG defaults on and SECRET_KEY has an insecure hardcoded default
findings.evidence: DEBUG = os.environ.get('DJANGO_DEBUG','1') == '1' (defaults True, line 19) and SECRET_KEY defaults to 'django-insecure-hd-6f2b1c9a4d7e0b5318ca77e2049fbd6c' (lines 21-24).
findings.impact: DEBUG=True leaks settings/stack traces/SQL to any error-triggering client; a known SECRET_KEY lets an attacker forge signed sessions, password-reset tokens and any signed value — session/account takeover.
findings.recommendation: Default DEBUG=False; require SECRET_KEY from the environment and fail closed if unset; rotate the leaked key.

triage.reason: Hardcoded SECRET_KEY is an intrinsic static-secret flaw retained by Rule 08.
A known signing key plus debug leakage are directly exploitable (signed-token forgery, secret disclosure), not passive hygiene.

findings.title: Session and CSRF cookies transmitted without Secure flag
findings.evidence: SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = False and CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = False (lines 118-119); comment says the last hop to app servers is plain http.
findings.impact: Session/CSRF cookies can be sent over http, exposing them to network sniffing on any non-TLS hop or downgrade.
findings.recommendation: Set both to True and terminate TLS end-to-end (or to the app tier); rely on the proxy only for external TLS, not the cookie boundary.

triage.reason: Kept as a real exposure of the auth cookie on the cleartext internal hop, though severity is low given the documented TLS-terminating proxy.

findings.title: SECURITY DEFINER function post_journal lacks a fixed search_path
findings.evidence: post_journal is SECURITY DEFINER (owned by ledger_owner) but, unlike archive_account which sets SET search_path = ledger, pg_temp, it has NO search_path pin. It references unqualified objects/functions (journals, entries, audit_log, current_setting, jsonb_array_elements).
findings.impact: The calling role (ledger_app) can prepend a schema it controls to search_path so unqualified names resolve to attacker objects executed as the definer (ledger_owner), enabling privilege escalation / arbitrary action as owner. The deliberate contrast with archive_account confirms the omission.
findings.recommendation: Add SET search_path = ledger, pg_temp to post_journal (and schema-qualify all object references), matching archive_account.

triage.reason: Missing search_path on a SECURITY DEFINER function is a well-known intrinsic Postgres escalation flaw, valid on the routine's own definition.
Full exploitation depends on the caller's CREATE rights (public schema is locked down in 004_grants.sql); not reproducible offline without a live cluster, so held probable.

findings.title: provision.sh fetches out-of-band migrations over plaintext HTTP and applies them as schema owner
findings.evidence: MIGRATION_MIRROR="http://artifacts.internal.example/ledger/migrations" (line 17); curl -fsSL over http downloads latest.tar.gz (line 48), tar -xzf extracts it, and the staged *.sql are run with psql -U ledger_owner (lines 82-86). No signature/checksum, no TLS.
findings.impact: A network MITM (or spoofed internal host) serves malicious SQL that provision.sh executes as ledger_owner — arbitrary schema/data control and privilege escalation on every deploy.
findings.recommendation: Fetch over https with certificate verification and verify a detached signature/checksum of the tarball before extracting; pin the artifact source.

triage.reason: The migration payload comes from an untrusted network channel (unauthenticated http) and is executed as owner; the source is attacker-influenceable via MITM.
Not mere hygiene: cleartext fetch feeding a privileged SQL executor is a concrete code-execution path.

findings.title: db.env containing the DB password is written world-readable (0644)
findings.evidence: The heredoc writes LEDGER_DB_PASSWORD into ${CONFIG_DIR}/db.env, then chmod 0644 makes it readable by every local user; comment notes multiple accounts read it and 'do not share a group'.
findings.impact: Any local user on the host reads the ledger_app DB password, bypassing the intended role/RLS boundary.
findings.recommendation: chmod 0640 (or 0600) with an appropriate owner/group; grant read via group membership rather than world-readable.

triage.reason: World-readable credential file is a concrete local disclosure, not a theoretical hygiene nit.
Any local (untrusted-relative-to-DB) user is an attacker able to read the secret at this sink.

findings.title: Export directory made world-writable (chmod -R 0777)
findings.evidence: chmod -R 0777 "$EXPORT_DIR" (/srv/ledger/exports) so every local user can read, modify, replace or delete statement bundles picked up by the reporting/archiver/ops jobs.
findings.impact: Local users can tamper with or plant files consumed by downstream jobs (integrity loss, possible code/content injection into archives) and read exported financial statements.
findings.recommendation: Use a shared group with 0770 and setgid, not 0777; grant per-service access explicitly.

triage.reason: World-writable shared directory consumed by other jobs is an exploitable integrity/confidentiality gap, not benign hardening.
Downstream impact depends on how consumers treat the files; not reproducible offline, held at probable.

findings.title: Session cookie is unsigned base64 JSON — full authentication and role forgery
findings.evidence: readSession base64url-decodes the nw_session cookie and JSON.parses it with NO signature/MAC check; writeSession (line 50) just base64-encodes JSON. userId, workspaceId and role are taken verbatim (role==='admin' honored).
findings.impact: Any user crafts a cookie {userId, workspaceId:<any>, role:'admin', issuedAt:now} to impersonate any user, become admin, and pivot to any workspace's data (server actions trust session.workspaceId). Middleware also copies the forged userId into the x-nw-user header. Complete auth/tenant bypass.
findings.recommendation: Sign the session (HMAC/JWT with a server secret) and verify it in readSession, or use a server-side session store keyed by an opaque random id; httpOnly does not provide integrity.

triage.reason: The cookie value is entirely attacker-authored and consumed as identity/role with no integrity gate; ingress is fully untrusted.
Trusting an unauthenticated token as a security principal is an intrinsic auth-logic flaw, independent of callers.

findings.title: /api/share is unauthenticated (excluded from middleware) and reads any note by id
findings.evidence: middleware.ts matcher '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico).*)' excludes all /api routes, so the auth wall never runs for /api/share. The POST handler reads the note via getNote(body.noteId) (line 30, unscoped by workspace/owner) and requires no session (readSession result only labels shared_by). It then POSTs note.title/html to the caller-chosen (allowlisted) target.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated attacker who knows/guesses a note id exfiltrates that note's content to one of the workspace's integration hosts, across workspace boundaries — no login required.
findings.recommendation: Require a valid session in the route handler and scope getNote to the caller's workspace/ownership; do not rely on middleware for /api routes it does not match.

triage.reason: noteId and target are attacker-controlled request-body fields; the route sits outside the auth boundary (middleware excludes /api) so untrusted input reaches the note-read sink.
The handler itself omits the authz check; no hypothetical misuse by a caller is required.

findings.title: updateNoteAction updates any note by id without workspace/ownership check
findings.evidence: updateNoteAction calls currentSession() (auth presence only) then getNote(input.id!) and saveNote(input.id!, ...) using the client-supplied id with no check that the note belongs to session.workspaceId (contrast createNoteAction which scopes to session.workspaceId).
findings.impact: Any authenticated user can overwrite the title/source/html of any other workspace's note by id — cross-tenant integrity loss (and a stored-content vector into other workspaces).
findings.recommendation: Load the note and assert existing.workspace_id === session.workspaceId (or filter the UPDATE by workspace_id) before saving; return 404 otherwise.

triage.reason: input.id is attacker-controlled form data reaching the update sink with no ownership boundary enforced.
The action itself skips the scope check; not a caller-side misuse assumption.

findings.title: Middleware reflects arbitrary Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
findings.evidence: For every matched (non-api) request the middleware sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the request's own Origin (line 16) and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true (line 17), with Vary: Origin — an unconditional reflect-with-credentials.
findings.impact: Any third-party site can make credentialed cross-origin requests to the workspace pages/RSC endpoints and read responses using the victim's cookie, enabling cross-site data theft.
findings.recommendation: Reflect only Origins on an explicit allowlist (the desktop/extension/marketing origins) before enabling credentials; otherwise omit ACAC.

triage.reason: The reflected Origin is attacker-controlled; combined with credentials it crosses the same-origin trust boundary.
Credentialed origin reflection is the exploit primitive itself, not a missing-header hardening item.

findings.title: Dead legacy session verifier uses salted MD5
findings.evidence: verifyLegacySession computes createHash('md5').update(salt + payload) and compares with '===' (line 67-69). No in-app caller (grep-confirmed); documented as used only by an out-of-repo backfill script.
findings.impact: If reused, MD5 with a simple salt||payload construction is vulnerable to collision/length-extension-style forgery and the '===' compare is not constant-time; weak session integrity.
findings.recommendation: Delete the dead function or replace with an HMAC-SHA-256 verify using timingSafeEqual.

triage.reason: Broken-hash (MD5) intrinsic flaw kept by Rule 08 even though the function is currently uncalled in this repo.
Exploitability depends on the external backfill script reusing it; not reproducible offline, held low.
